transcript.text: Sometimes when I open the dishwasher there's grey smelly water in the bottom even though it finished draining fine. Not every day though. Kitchen sink was replaced last month if that matters.

That grey, smelly water in the base after a cycle usually means either something is preventing it from draining fully, or water is trickling back into the machine from the sink waste. Given your kitchen sink was replaced recently, plumbing-related issues are quite possible. The most common cause is simply a partial blockage in the filter or sump area that lets some water through but leaves residue behind. Another strong possibility, especially with recent work on the sink, is that the blanking plug inside the new sink waste spigot wasn't removed, or the trap is partially blocked, causing slow drainage and odours. Let's start with the easiest check:
1. Switch off and unplug the dishwasher.
2. Remove the bottom rack and twist out the filter assembly at the base of the tub.
3. Look into the sump (the hole where the filter was) with a torch. Is there any food debris, glass, or grease blocking the small impeller (the little plastic fan-like part)? Also, is the filter itself clogged? Please let me know what you find in the sump and on the filter.
[Helpful to see: image "Where the filter is" — The filter sits in the base of the dishwasher, usually under the bottom spray arm. Twist it out anticlockwise and rinse it under a tap. Typical layout — your dishwasher may differ.]
I've taken the filter out and it's clean, nothing in the sump that I can see. The water seems to appear after I've drained the sink full of washing-up water, if that helps.

That pattern—water appearing specifically after you've drained a full sink of soapy water—points to the plumbing connection rather than the machine itself. The dishwasher is likely draining fine initially, but slow drainage or backflow from the sink waste is pushing dirty water back into the base. 1. The blanking plug inside the sink waste spigot (where the dishwasher hose connects) was left in place, restricting flow and causing gurgling/backflow.
2. The sink trap (U-bend) is partially blocked or not draining fast enough to handle a sudden large volume of water from the sink, forcing it back towards the lowest point—the dishwasher drain hose. 1. Look at the spigot where the dishwasher hose attaches. Is there a small plastic plug still inside?
2. Run the tap and see if the sink waste drains freely or if water pools in the U-bend/trap for a while. Let me know what you find with those two points.
I can't see any plug where the hose connects, but I'm not sure what I'd be looking for inside the spigot. The sink does drain a little slow when I run the tap, though it doesn't back up.

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. The fact that the water appears specifically after you run a large volume of soapy water from the sink, combined with the slow drainage you noticed earlier, suggests the sink waste plumbing is restricting flow. Even if there isn't a visible blockage or a missing blanking plug, the trap (U-bend) under the sink may be partially clogged with grease or debris, or the connection to the wall pipe might be tight. This restriction prevents water from leaving fast enough, causing it to back up into the lowest point—the dishwasher drain hose. The most effective next step is to check the trap itself:
1. Place a bucket under the U-bend (the curved pipe section) under the sink.
2. Loosen the slip nuts and remove the trap.
3. Clear out any sludge, hair, or debris inside it and rinse it through.
4. Reconnect it securely and run the tap to see if the flow improves significantly. If you are not comfortable doing this, try running a full sink of water and pulling the plug; if that drains much faster than just running the tap, the restriction is confirmed in the plumbing. Please let me know what happens when you check the trap or the full-sink drain.

I haven't taken the trap off yet. I'm fine with a bucket and slip nuts though. A full sink does drain a little slowly, but I can't really tell if it's faster than the tap. Is there anything else under the sink I should look at while I'm down there?

Yes, while you are under there, check two specific things: 1. The U-bend (trap): Is it full of sludge, hair, or debris? If it is, that suggests the slow drainage and explains why water backs up into the dishwasher when you run a lot of sink water.
2. The drain hose routing: Look at the grey hose running from the dishwasher to the sink spigot. Is it kinked, squashed flat, or pushed too far back into the wall pipe? A blocked or restricted hose will stop the dishwasher from draining properly even if the sink itself is clear. Please let me know what you find with those two checks.

Had a look at the hose. It's not kinked or squashed, but since the new sink went in it just lies on the cupboard floor and goes straight into the waste spigot. There's no high loop in it at all. I haven't checked the trap itself yet.

Even if there isn't a visible blockage or a missing blanking plug, the trap (U-bend) under the sink may be partially clogged with grease or debris, or the connection to the wall pipe might be tight. This restriction prevents water from leaving fast enough, causing it to back up into the lowest point—the dishwasher drain hose. The second issue is that without a high loop, gravity can pull dirty water back down the hose once the sink drains, especially if there's any slight restriction in the waste. The standard fix for this is to create a 'high loop' where the hose rises up towards the underside of the worktop before dropping into the sink waste. Please go ahead with clearing the trap as planned (bucket under U-bend, loosen slip nuts, clean it out). While you are down there, please also lift the dishwasher drain hose up so it forms a high loop (at least 20cm/8 inches above the floor) before it drops down into the waste spigot. Secure it with a clip or tie to the underside of the worktop. Let me know if clearing the trap improves the sink drainage and if you were able to create that loop.

I've looped the hose up high and clipped it under the worktop, and since then there's been no more water in the base. I haven't taken the trap off yet, so I can't say whether that makes the sink drain any faster.

That is excellent news. The lack of a high loop was most likely allowing dirty water to flow back into the machine when you ran the sink. Keeping that hose elevated ensures gravity works with you rather than against you. As one final tip: since your sink still drains a little slowly from the tap, I would recommend clearing that trap (U-bend) under the sink when you have time. Removing any grease or sludge there will stop the slow drainage and prevent any future backflow issues.
